vignette:
Chinedu's Story

Chinedu was nine years old when his uncle came to stay with them in Lagos. The man had rough hands—palms calloused and scarred from years working construction—and a temper that ignited without warning. One afternoon, after Chinedu spilled water on the kitchen floor, his uncle grabbed him by the wrist, his grip a vise of heat and pressure. The skin of his uncle's palm was coarse, almost like sandpaper, and it burned against Chinedu's forearm as he was dragged into the back room. The beating that followed lasted only minutes, but the sensations lingered: the texture of that rough palm, the suffocating warmth of the room, the sound of footsteps approaching from behind whenever his uncle moved through the house. By the time his mother sent his uncle away three months later, Chinedu had learned to flinch at the sound of approaching footsteps, to feel his heart race when someone's skin—rough or warm—made contact with his own.

Now, at twenty-seven, Chinedu had built a life in Atlanta that kept him moving. He drove for Uber five nights a week, a job that suited him because it meant solitude, control, and constant motion. But the city itself had become a minefield of invisible triggers. The texture of a passenger's wool coat brushing his arm in the backseat could send him spiraling; the warmth of another body in close quarters made his skin crawl. Footsteps on the pavement behind him—a pedestrian approaching his car, a neighbor walking down the hallway of his apartment building—would snap his attention backward, his shoulders tensing, his breath shallow. When these moments hit, the only way forward was to reach for his phone and scroll mindlessly through videos, anything to pull his attention away from the sensation still prickling on his skin; more frequently now, he was using cocaine before shifts, a habit that had started as occasional relief but had quietly become something he needed to get through the day. When these moments hit, Chinedu's first instinct was to reach for his phone and scroll mindlessly through videos, anything to pull his attention away from the sensation still prickling on his skin. The roughness of a stranger's coat, the sound of footsteps, the suffocating closeness of the backseat—each one sent him scrambling for distraction, and more frequently now, toward cocaine, a habit that had started as occasional relief and had quietly become something he needed before difficult shifts. These moments came without warning, and they came often. When a trigger hit, Chinedu's first instinct was to reach for his phone and scroll mindlessly through videos, anything to pull his attention away from the sensation still prickling on his skin. More frequently now, he was using cocaine—a habit that had started as occasional relief and had quietly become something he needed before difficult shifts. The drugs dulled the edge, made the world feel less sharp, less threatening. They also gave him something to focus on besides the fact that his body seemed determined to betray him, reacting as if danger were still present even when he knew, rationally, that he was safe in his apartment or alone in his car.

What frightened Chinedu most was the certainty that he had become irreparably broken. He had come to believe that something fundamental in him had shattered that day in Lagos, that no amount of time or distance would mend it. Because he was convinced he was damaged beyond repair, he could not imagine letting anyone close; his sister's invitations to family gatherings had been declined for two years, and the few women who had shown interest in him were met with coldness and withdrawal, as if isolation were the only honest thing to do, a way of protecting others from what he had become. His body had turned against him—it kept reacting as if his uncle were still there, still reaching for him, still threatening. Because he believed he was damaged beyond repair, he could not imagine letting anyone close; his sister's invitations to family gatherings had been declined for two years, and the few women who had shown interest in him were met with coldness and withdrawal. If he was truly broken, then isolation was not avoidance—it was the only honest thing to do, a way of protecting others from what he had become. Even when passengers were kind, even when his sister called to check on him, even when he sat alone in his apartment with the doors locked, he could not silence the alarm bells ringing in his nervous system. The fact that his body insisted on threat even in objectively safe moments—that he could not trust his own nervous system to distinguish danger from safety—quietly confirmed what he had come to believe about himself: that something fundamental in him had broken, that he was not the kind of person who got to feel secure. When his body insisted on threat even in objectively safe moments, the only way Chinedu had found to move through the world was to numb it—the cocaine dulled the edge, made the world feel less sharp, less threatening, and gave him something to focus on besides the fact that he could not trust his own nervous system. He was also driving too fast on empty highways at night, taking passengers in neighborhoods he knew were dangerous, staying out until dawn without sleep, as if the intensity of the threat he felt justified reckless action. This conviction fed everything else. Because he believed he was damaged beyond repair, because he felt unsafe even in objectively safe situations, he stopped trying to let people close. His sister had invited him to family gatherings, and he had declined every invitation for the past two years. The few women who had shown interest in him were met with coldness and withdrawal; he could not bear the thought of being touched, of being vulnerable, of someone discovering just how broken he really was. His hypervigilance—the constant scanning for threat, the way his eyes tracked movement in his rearview mirror, the way he sat with his back to the wall—had become exhausting and inescapable. Even when he was objectively safe, his mind and body insisted otherwise, and that impossibility of trusting safety, of ever truly relaxing, only deepened his conviction that he was permanently changed.

The hypervigilance and the inability to trust safety fed a reckless streak that had begun to alarm him. He was driving too fast on empty highways at night, taking passengers in neighborhoods he knew were dangerous, staying out until dawn without sleep. Part of him felt invincible, as if he had already been damaged so thoroughly that nothing worse could happen. Another part of him, quieter and more terrifying, wondered if he was unconsciously courting harm. The cocaine use had accelerated in recent weeks, and with it came a growing sense of isolation. He had lost touch with the Nigerian community he had once felt tethered to—the church his mother attended, the friends from university who still gathered on weekends. He could not explain to them why he could not be around people, why a casual touch made him recoil, why he was not the person they remembered. Each time he declined an invitation, each time he used cocaine to get through a shift, each time he pulled away from someone trying to reach him, the evidence accumulated silently: he must be more broken than other people, or he would have been able to do these things by now. The avoidance and the drugs had become proof of the very thing he feared most—that he was irreparably changed. The drugs and the distraction, the avoidance of intimacy and the constant movement, had become a wall between him and everything that had once felt like home.

It was his sister who finally pushed him to seek help. She had noticed the weight loss, the tremor in his hands, the way he flinched when she tried to hug him. She had also learned, through a mutual friend, about the cocaine. When she confronted him three weeks ago, Chinedu had no defense—only the exhausted admission that he could not keep living this way, that something had to change. What he feared most was that therapy would confirm what he already believed: that he was beyond repair. What he hoped for, though he barely dared speak it aloud, was that someone might help him understand why his body would not believe he was safe, and whether there was any way to reclaim even a fraction of the person he had been before his uncle arrived.

He had lost touch with the Nigerian community he had once felt tethered to—the church his mother attended, the friends from university who still gathered on weekends. He could not explain to them why he could not be around people, why a casual touch made him recoil, why he was not the person they remembered. Each time he declined an invitation, each time he used cocaine to get through a shift, each time he pulled away from someone trying to reach him, the evidence accumulated silently: he must be more broken than other people, or he would have been able to do these things by now. The avoidance and the drugs had become proof of the very thing he feared most—that he was irreparably changed. The drugs and the distraction, the avoidance of intimacy and the constant movement, had become a wall between him and everything that had once felt like home.

It was his sister who finally pushed him to seek help. She had noticed the weight loss, the tremor in his hands, the way he flinched when she tried to hug him. She had also learned, through a mutual friend, about the cocaine. When she confronted him three weeks ago, Chinedu had no defense—only the exhausted admission that he could not keep living this way, that something had to change. What he feared most was that therapy would confirm what he already believed: that he was beyond repair. What he hoped for, though he barely dared speak it aloud, was that someone might help him understand why his body would not believe he was safe, and whether there was any way to reclaim even a fraction of the person he had been before his uncle arrived.
